text: We study a nonlinear split feasibility problem whose output set is a normal box and whose component functions are differentiable and each convex or pseudoconvex.
We propose the Dual-Track Adaptive Projection (DTAP) algorithm, which splits the constraints into a convex and a pseudoconvex track and works on the nearly most violated constraints of each.

DTAP combines a residual-scaled Polyak-type step on the convex track with a safeguarded diminishing step on the pseudoconvex track through a residual-responsive proportional weight, and then projects onto the base convex set.
Its step sizes require no prescribed operator norm, Lipschitz constant, or Hölder modulus; the proof uses local bounds on the bounded iterate region.
Under consistency and continuous differentiability, we prove that the whole sequence converges strongly to a feasible point.
As an application, we formulate feature selection as such a problem, with constraints built from fractional and fuzzy-rough feature-selection criteria.

Experiments on UCI datasets show that the selected features keep the classification accuracy close to that of the full feature set, and test problems with a nonconvex pseudoconvex constraint exercise the pseudoconvex track; we also compare DTAP with subgradient methods and study its sensitivity to the starting point and the step scale.

Assumptions
We assume (A1)--(A3):
(a) $\Omega\ne\emptyset$ (consistency).
(b) $I=\{1,\dots,m\}$ is partitioned as $I=I^{\cvx}\cup I^{\ps}$; each $F_i:U\to\R$ is convex on $K$ if $i\in I^{\cvx}$ and pseudoconvex on $K$ if $i\in I^{\ps}$.
Each $F_i:U\to\R$ is continuously differentiable on $U$.
(i) $\delta>0$ fixed.
(iii) $\{\gamma_k\}\subset(0,\infty)$ with $\sum_{k=0}^\infty\gamma_k^2<\infty$ and $\sum_{k=0}^\infty\gamma_k=\infty$.
The open-neighbourhood formulation permits fractional functions whose denominators are positive on $K$; the algorithm evaluates the functions and gradients only at points of $K$.
Although some component functions may be nonconvex, $\Omega$ is convex: differentiable pseudoconvex functions are quasiconvex on $K$, so all constraint sublevel sets in $K$ are convex.
The sequence $\gamma_k:=1/(k+1)$ satisfies (A3)(iii), since $\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)^{-2}<\infty$ while $\sum_{k\ge0}(k+1)^{-1}=\infty$.
More generally $\gamma_k=(k+c)^{-s}$ with $c>0$ and $s\in(1/2,1]$ qualifies; the experiments use $s=0.55$.
The DTAP algorithm
The Dual-Track Adaptive Projection algorithm combines the two track-specific step sizes through the proportional weight $\mu_k$ and projects the combined update onto the base convex set $K$.

The proportional weight is an adaptive allocation based on the two maximal violations; we do not claim that it is the only choice for which DTAP converges, or that it is optimal.

The iteration does not require prescribed operator norms, Lipschitz constants, or Hölder moduli.
The proof nevertheless uses finite bounds on function values and gradients on a compact set containing the iterates, after boundedness has been proved.
Bounded gradients imply Lipschitz continuity of the functions on that convex compact set, but these bounds are not algorithm inputs.
Assumption (A2) does not imply Lipschitz continuity of the gradients, and the theorem does not require it.
The user still chooses $\rho_{\cvx}$, $\delta$, and $\{\gamma_k\}$; these parameters do not depend on any constant of the problem.
For the analysis we write the combined increment as [công thức (16)] so $y^k=x^k-d_k$ and $x^{k+1}=P_K(x^k-d_k)$.
Per-iteration cost

Each DTAP iteration evaluates the componentwise violations $v_i(x^k)$ and the active-set gradients $\{\nabla F_i(x^k):i\in K^{\cvx}_k\cup K^{\ps}_k\}$, forms the two search directions $g^{\cvx}_k,g^{\ps}_k$ as weighted sums of these gradients, computes the step sizes, and performs one projection onto $K$.
It uses neither an operator-norm estimate nor a line search.
The cost is dominated by the constraint evaluations and the projection.
The cost for the feature-selection instance is given in Section 4.1 (Remark 6).

To solve the fractional program (34), Wang et al. [15] proposed a neurodynamic method coupling a projection neural network (PNN) with a $k$-winners-take-all network.

The PNN is the differential system [công thức (45)] with output $w=g(u)$, where $g(u)=\max\{0,u\}$ is the componentwise ReLU, $\Pi=\tfrac1p\mathbf{1}_p\mathbf{1}_p^{\top}$, $\nabla f$ is the gradient of the objective in (34), and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{PNN}}>0$ is a time constant.

Conclusion
DTAP solves normal-box nonlinear split feasibility problems with convex and pseudoconvex components by combining a residual-scaled convex step with a safeguarded pseudoconvex step.

Under consistency and continuous differentiability, the whole sequence converges to a feasible point; no regularity modulus is an input, although the analysis uses bounds on a compact set containing the iterates.
In the feature-selection application all constraints are convex, and test problems with a nonconvex pseudoconvex constraint exercise the pseudoconvex track.
In the experiments, tuned subgradient methods can match or outperform DTAP, whose finite-budget performance depends on the starting point and the step scale.
Rates for the full residual $J(x^k)$, beyond the convex-track bound of Remark 5, and guarantees under error-bound conditions remain open.
